prep:in.tx: From Middle High German in, from Old High German in.

adj:ideal.tx: Borrowed from Late Latin ideālis (“existing in idea”), from Latin idea (“idea”). Doublet of ideell.

adj:instrumental.tx: Borrowed from French instrumental. Equivalent to Instrument + -al.

pron:ich.tx: From Middle High German ich, from Old High German ih, from Proto-West Germanic *ik, from Proto-Germanic *ek, *ik, from Proto-Indo-European *eǵh₂óm.

adj:intelligent.tx: From Latin intellegēns (“discerning”), present active participle of intellegō (“understand, comprehend”), itself from inter (“between”) + legō (“choose, pick out, read”).

noun:Israeli.tx: From Hebrew יִשְׂרְאֵלִי, equivalent to Israel + -i.

pron:ihr.tx: From Middle High German ir, from Old High German ir, from Proto-West Germanic *jiʀ, from Proto-Germanic *jīz. Cognate with Low German ji, jie, Yiddish איר (ir), Dutch jij, gij, je, Middle Dutch ir, English ye, Gothic 𐌾𐌿𐍃 (jūs).

det:ihr.tx: From Old High German ira, from Proto-Germanic *hezōi.

noun:Insel.tx: From Middle High German insel, insele, isele, from Old High German isila, *insila, from Proto-West Germanic *isulā, *insulā, borrowed from Latin *isula, insula (“island”). Native Middle High German words for “island” were ouwe and wert; cf. modern Aue (“meadow by a river”) and Werder (“river island”). Other borrowings were eilant, einlant (from Old Frisian; see Eiland) and the rare īle (from Old …

adj:inferior.tx: Borrowed from Latin īnferior (“lower, inferior”), the comparative of īnferus (“low, nether, underground”).

adj:indifferent.tx: 17th century, from Latin indifferens, mostly through French indifférent.

adj:insane.tx: Borrowed from English insane. Doublet of insan.

adj:international.tx: From English international. By surface analysis, inter- + national.

noun:Idol.tx: Borrowed from Latin īdōlum, from Ancient Greek εἴδωλον (eídōlon). Used in German chiefly since the 18th century, before that occasionally as an ad-hoc borrowing from the Latin.

noun:Illustration.tx: Borrowed from Latin illūstrātiō in the 1800s, from illūstrō (“to illustrate”).

noun:Imagination.tx: Borrowed from French imagination, from Latin imāginātiō.

noun:Indigo.tx: From Spanish índigo, from Latin indicus.

noun:Inland.tx: 19th century, from in- + Land, a back-formation from Ausland as well as from older Inländer, inländisch (themselves backformations from Ausländer, ausländisch).

noun:Inspiration.tx: Learned 16th century borrowing from Late Latin īnspīrātiō, from Latin īnspīrātus, perfect participle of īnspīrō (“to breathe in, to inhale”), + -tiō.

noun:Instrument.tx: From Middle High German instrument, from Latin īnstrūmentum. Compare Middle Low German instrument (whence German Low German Instrument), Middle English instrument (whence English instrument), Middle Dutch instrument (whence Dutch instrument).

noun:Ion.tx: Borrowed from English ion, indirectly from Ancient Greek ἰόν (ión, “wandering”).

pron:icke.tx: Borrowed from Low German ick, from Proto-Germanic *ek, from Proto-Indo-European *eǵh₂óm.

noun:Inferno.tx: Borrowed from Italian inferno, from Latin īnfernus (locus) (“hell”). Adopted in the context of Dante’s Inferno. Freer use chiefly since the 19th century.

adj:insolvent.tx: 17th century, from Dutch insolvent (1582). Equivalent to in- + solvent. The latter is younger in German.

adv:immer.tx: From Middle High German iemer (also imer, immer), from Old High German iomēr (“always”). Cognate with Dutch immer, Alemannic German immer, German Low German immer, ümmer, jümmer, jümmers, Middle English a mare, aa mare (“evermore”).

adv:inne.tx: From Middle High German inne, from Old High German inne, from Proto-Germanic *innai. Compare Old English inne.

noun:Igel.tx: From Middle High German igel, from Old High German igil, from Proto-West Germanic *igil, from Proto-Germanic *igilaz, diminutive of Proto-Indo-European *h₁eǵʰis (“hedgehog”), *h₁eǵʰ-io- (compare Lithuanian ežỹs, Armenian ոզնի (ozni)).

noun:Imbiss.tx: From Middle High German imbiz, imbīz, inbīz (“food, meal, snack, breakfast”), from Old High German inbiz, inbīz, imbīz (“food, meal, snack”), equivalent to in- (“in, into”) + Biss (“bite”). Compare German Low German Anbiet (“meal, snack”), Dutch ontbijt (“breakfast”).

noun:Imker.tx: From German Low German Imker. Obviously related to Imme (“bee”). There are two theories concerning the details of the development: # From Middle Low German immenkar (“beehive”), which is a compound with Middle Low German kar (“basket”). The component -ker < -kar would then have been secondarily associated with the Low German suffix -ker for occupations (compare Böttcher). # Directly derived from …

noun:Imme.tx: From Middle High German imbe (“bee; swarm of bees”), from Old High German imbi (“swarm of bees”). Cognate with Bavarian Imp.

verb:impfen.tx: From Middle High German impfen (“to graft”), from Old High German impfōn (impitōn), from Proto-West Germanic *impōn, from Vulgar Latin *imputō (“to graft”) (unrelated to imputō (“to reckon, attribute”)), from Ancient Greek ἔμφυτος (émphutos, “planted”). Compare English imp.

noun:Ingwer.tx: From Middle High German ingewer, ingeber, from Old High German ingiber, gingiber, gingibero, from Proto-West Germanic *gingiberō.

adj:irre.tx: From Middle High German irre, erre, from Old High German irri, from Proto-West Germanic *irʀī, from Proto-Germanic *irzijaz (“bewildered, confused, crazy, lost”). Related to irren (“to wander, get lost”).

adj:immens.tx: Borrowed from French immense, or possibly directly from Latin immēnsus.

verb:irren.tx: From Middle High German irren, from Old High German irren, from Proto-West Germanic *irʀijan, from Proto-Germanic *irzijaną.

noun:Intelligenz.tx: Borrowed from Latin intelligentia (“intelligence”), a variant of intellegentia.

noun:Identität.tx: Borrowed from Medieval Latin identitās (“sameness, identity”) in the 18th century, from Latin īdem (“the same”).

noun:Impfung.tx: From Early New High German impfung, imptung, from Middle High German impfetunge, imptunge, from Old High German imphunga. Equivalent to impfen + -ung.

noun:Idee.tx: Borrowed from French idée, from Latin idea (“a (Platonic) idea; archetype”), from Ancient Greek ἰδέα (idéa, “notion, pattern”), from εἴδω (eídō, “to see”).

noun:Interesse.tx: From Medieval Latin interesse under influence of French intérêt.

verb:investieren.tx: Late Middle High German, from Latin investīre. In the finance sense from Italian investire or English invest.

noun:Inschrift.tx: 15th century, common since the 18th century. From in- + Schrift, a calque of Latin inscriptio. The according verb is einschreiben, so one might expect Einschrift (which is well attested); the in-form possibly under direct influence of the Latin word.

noun:Internat.tx: Borrowed from French internat. By surface analysis, intern + -at.

pron:ick.tx: Borrowed from Low German ick, ik. Doublet of ich.

verb:importieren.tx: 18th century, from English import, from Latin importare. Analysable as Import + -ieren.

noun:Imperialismus.tx: Borrowed from French impérialisme, originally “support for the imperial form of government”.

adj:intrigant.tx: Borrowed from French intrigant. Equivalent to Intrige + -ant.

noun:Intrigant.tx: Borrowed from French intrigant. Equivalent to Intrige + -ant.

noun:Irrtum.tx: From Middle High German irretuom, from Old High German irrituom. Equivalent to irren (“to wander”) + -tum. Related to English error via the same Proto-Indo-European root (though the English is borrowed from the Italic cognate).

intj:igitt.tx: 19th century, of northern German origin. Probably a minced oath/veiled use of a phrase like o Gott (“oh God!”), compare oh God. Or, an extended form of (the presumably imitative) ih (“ew, yuck; sound of disgust”), possibly influenced by the former.

verb:interpretieren.tx: From French interpréter + -ieren, from Old French enterpreter, from Latin interpretor (“to explain, expound, interpret”).

adj:illusorisch.tx: Adapted borrowing of French illusoire + -isch, from Latin illūsōrius.

verb:imprägnieren.tx: From French imprégner and/or Latin impraegnō + -ieren.

noun:Interieur.tx: Borrowed from French intérieur, from Latin interior.

verb:inszenieren.tx: From in- + Szene + -ieren. Compare Italian inscenare.

adj:ideell.tx: Borrowed from French idéel, from Late Latin ideālis (“existing in idea”), from Latin idea (“idea”). Doublet of ideal.

noun:Importeur.tx: 19th century, from French importeur, now archaic variant of importateur. Equivalent to importieren + -eur.

noun:Industrie.tx: Borrowed from French industrie, from Latin industria.

verb:integrieren.tx: Clearly borrowed, ultimately from Latin integro, likely through French intégrer.

adj:infam.tx: From Latin īnfāmis, partly through French infâme.

adv:inzwischen.tx: From Middle High German enzwischen, from Old High German in zwiskēn or in zuiskēn. By surface analysis, in + zwischen. Equivalent to Dutch intussen.

noun:Ischias.tx: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἰσχιάς (iskhiás, “hip disease”), from ἰσχίον (iskhíon, “hip joint”).

noun:Ikone.tx: Borrowed from Russian икона (ikona). Doublet of Icon.

verb:implizieren.tx: Borrowed from Latin implicāre. Doublet of einflechten.

verb:inhalieren.tx: 19th century, from Latin inhalare, in part through French inhaler.

adj:inzestuös.tx: Derived from Inzest + -ös, on the model of French incestueux.

adv:indes.tx: From Middle High German innen des. Compare indessen.

conj:indes.tx: From Middle High German innen des. Compare indessen.

noun:Iltis.tx: From Middle High German iltis, from Old High German illitiso, illintiso, of uncertain origin. Perhaps a compound from the Proto-Indo-European roots *h₁el- (“red, brown”) and *weys- (“to flow, run”). The latter was probably used for animal secretions, whence the noun *wiso- or *wisós (“fluidity, slime, reek, poison”), as in Wiesel and Wisent; compare Ancient Greek ἰός (iós) and Latin virus.

noun:Isotop.tx: From iso- + -top, from Ancient Greek τόπος (tópos).

verb:innehalten.tx: From Middle High German inne halten, inhalten. Equivalent to inne- + halten, literally “to hold in”.

adj:irdisch.tx: From Middle High German irdisch, from Old High German irdisc, irdisk, derived from ërda, whence modern Erde (“earth”).

adj:indiskutabel.tx: From in- + diskutabel, after French indiscutable.

noun:Inselaffe.tx: From Insel + Affe, literally “island monkey”. The word Affe is used in German both for boorish, rowdy persons and for affected, hoity-toity persons (compare affig, Lackaffe, indirectly also affektiert). Both of these qualities are sometimes associated with (different classes of) English people.

prep:inmitten.tx: From Middle High German enmitten, enmittent, from Old High German in mitten.

adj:inmitten.tx: From Middle High German enmitten, enmittent, from Old High German in mitten.

adv:infolgedessen.tx: Univerbation of infolge + dessen. Compare Dutch dientengevolge.

adj:instabil.tx: 18th century, from Latin instabilis. Equivalent to in- + stabil.

noun:Insasse.tx: From Middle High German īnsæʒe (“inhabitant, tenant”), from Middle Low German insāte, insēte (“inhabitant”); related to Eingesessener. Ultimately from the root of sitzen (“to sit”).

adv:intus.tx: Borrowed from Latin intus (“inside”). Originally in the slang of students, 19th century.

noun:Installateur.tx: From French installateur (“installer”) with a shift in meaning.

noun:Inbetriebnahme.tx: Verbal noun of in Betrieb nehmen (“to put into operation”). Analysable as in + Betrieb + Nahme.

noun:Inbesitznahme.tx: Nominalization of in Besitz nehmen with Nahme as the deverbal for nehmen, 19th century.

adv:immerhin.tx: Univerbation of immer (“always”) + hin (“(to) there, onwards”), originally in a temporal sense of an ongoing action or state, or figuratively encouragement thereof, from which a contrastive sense developed.

noun:Immatrikulation.tx: From immatrikulieren, from Medieval Latin immātrīculāre.

noun:ISIS.tx: Abbreviation of Islamischer Staat im Irak und (in) (Groß-)Syrien

noun:Instanz.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin īnstantia (“perseverence, urgency”), first referring to the pursuit of a legal matter, then the office responsible for that pursuit. The technological sense is a later semantic loan from English instance.

adv:irgend.tx: From Middle High German irgent, iergen (“somewhere”), from Old High German io wergin, hwergin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hwargin.

adv:ihretwegen.tx: Shortened from von ihretwegen, which can be traced through two developmental routes. One route is from von ihrentwegen / von ihrent wegen, from von ihren wegen, from Middle High German von irn wegen, in which wegen was the dative plural of modern-day Weg and irn was the possessive pronoun in the dative plural. Another route can be traced from von ihrtwegen / von ihrt wegen, from Middle High …

noun:Inspektion.tx: 16th century, learned borrowing from Latin īnspectiō.

noun:Interpunktion.tx: Borrowed from Latin interpūnctiō (“dividing words by periods”).

noun:Inbusschlüssel.tx: Compound of the trademark Inbus (abbreviation of “Innensechskantschraube Bauer und Schaurte”) of the company Bauer & Schaurte and Schlüssel (“key”). The term has entered generic usage.

phrase:in China fällt ein Sack Reis um.tx: Apparently first coined during an interview of a soccer fan club in Hamburg in 1980.

adj:inbrünstig.tx: From Late Middle High German inbrünstec.

adv:inbrünstig.tx: From Late Middle High German inbrünstec.

verb:inlinern.tx: Derived from Inliner, itself from Inlineskate.

phrase:in spe.tx: Borrowed from Latin in spē (literally “in [the] hope; hopeful”).

adj:inständig.tx: Partial calque of Latin instanter (“insistently, vehemently”), from the 16th century. Probably influenced by adjectives like beständig and anständig.

noun:Itzig.tx: Borrowed from Yiddish איציק (itsik), a variant or pet form of the name Isaak.

noun:Instruktor.tx: Borrowed from Latin īnstrūctor. Doublet of Instrukteur.

noun:Instrukteur.tx: Borrowed from French instructeur. Doublet of Instruktor.

noun:Infusion.tx: Borrowed from Latin infusio, from Latin infundō.

pron:icht.tx: From Middle High German iht, icht, ieht, from Old High German iowiht. Cognate with Dutch iet, English aught.

noun:Itaker.tx: First attested in the 1960s, from the military slang term Itaka, an abbreviation of italienischer Kamerad (“Italian comrade”). Similar forms have been used as early as World War I.

noun:Icon.tx: Borrowed from English icon. Doublet of Ikone.

noun:Insolenz.tx: Borrowed from French insolence, from Latin insolentia.

noun:Ische.tx: From Hebrew אישה (ishá, “woman”) via Yiddish [Term?] or Rotwelsch.

noun:Illegaler.tx: Adjectival noun from illegal, often implying Migrant, Ausländer etc. depending on the context.

phrase:in dubio pro reo.tx: Borrowed from Latin. Literally, “in case of doubt in favour of the accused”.

noun:Insiderhandel.tx: Partial calque of English insider trading.

noun:Infarkt.tx: Borrowed from Latin īnfarctus, tu-stem derivation of īnfarciō.

noun:Innung.tx: From Middle High German innunge, derived from Old High German innōn (“to accept, let enter”), from in.

phrase:ich sehe was, was du nicht siehst.tx: Literally, “I see something that you don't see”. Compare Dutch ik zie, ik zie wat jij niet ziet.

noun:ITC.tx: Derived from English ITCZ (“Intertropical convergence zone”)

noun:Insuffizienz.tx: From Latin insufficientia, from Latin in- + sufficere. See also insuffizient.

prep:innert.tx: From earlier inret, from Middle High German inrent. Probably equivalent to inneren (dative of inner) with paragogic -t.

noun:Inanspruchnahme.tx: From in Anspruch nehmen (“to claim, take up”).

phrase:immer feste druff.tx: Title of an operetta by Walter Kollo (1914).

phrase:in der Not schmeckt die Wurst auc.tx: Literally, “in [times of] need, sausage tastes [good] even without bread”, jocular alteration of in der Not schmeckt jedes Brot.

noun:Intrusion.tx: Borrowed from Medieval Latin intrūsiō, from Latin intrūdō.

noun:Investmentfonds.tx: Borrowed from English investment fund. Surface analysis yields Investment (“investment”) + Fonds (“fund”).

noun:Immobilienvermögen.tx: Immobilie (“real estate; property”) + -n- (“plural interfix”) + Vermögen (“assets; wealth”)

noun:Immanenz.tx: From Latin immanēns, from Latin immaneō (“to indwell”).
